**Opening argument for debater B: the maximum is max{C(n−1,2)+k, (k+1)(n−1)−1}**

**Upper bound via Nash-Williams–Tutte.** A graph has k+1 edge-disjoint spanning trees iff every vertex partition P satisfies e(P) ≥ (k+1)(|P|−1), where e(P) counts cross-part edges. So a graph without them has some partition with e(P) ≤ (k+1)(p−1)−1, where p = |P|. Its total edge count is at most C(n−p+1, 2) + (k+1)(p−1) − 1, since the parts can hold at most C(n−p+1, 2) internal edges when one part is as large as possible. This bound is convex in p, so its maximum over 2 ≤ p ≤ n sits at an endpoint. p = 2 gives C(n−1,2)+k, and p = n gives (k+1)(n−1)−1. This is exactly the claimed formula.

**Extremal constructions.**
- For n ≥ 2k+3: take K_{n−1} plus a vertex of degree k. The partition {v} vs. the rest has only k cross edges, so there are no k+1 trees. Adding any edge at v restores them, giving C(n−1,2)+k edges.
- For n = 2k+2: K_n minus one edge has (k+1)(n−1)−1 = C(n,2)−1 edges. The singleton partition is short by one, so the graph fails, and adding the missing edge gives K_n, which succeeds.

**Consistency checks.** At n = 2k+3 both terms equal 2k²+4k+1. Beyond that, the quadratic term dominates, so the switch in the maximum is exactly at the stated thresholds.
